title: Houston, Wichita Falls, the Louisiana Ramblers, California and Werlein's
summary: One long account of offers by telegram, the Louisiana Ramblers, going to California with Teagarden and Doc Ross, and choosing the music store business around 1926.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: And, it was Jack and Terry Sheehan up in, uh, Thomas John, and William Gramsson, and all that stuff. And, they played all the society dances, and they played the Fiori roof garden. And, this particular man, this guy, who I was talking about, uh, was, uh, Asian. He hired them. And, uh, so I guess the buddies then, uh, who, uh, who, uh, were, uh, uh, who, uh, were included the Red Round Tree and Buddy Seeky and drums and, um, who included Red Roundtree and Buddy Seaton on drums and Shockey Wilcox on trumpet. And Red Roundtree was a very famous banjo player who played with Lute Speed, and he was at the Arcade Studios in California for 20 years, and he's still living. And I had recently been out to see him and jammed with me at all. So the Buddies then, after the Buddies broke up, I had several offers to join different bands. So I went to Houston for a little while and played at what's called Basho Park. And I always kicked myself because Jack and Peck were playing with Galveston, which was not more than 50 miles away than they would get together. At that time. But so much of my history ties in with Snoozer and Jack and Peck, although I didn't work with Peck, but I was first years. And he came up the street to it. So after I went to Houston, I went out to Wichita Falls, Texas, and played with the 80s trumpeters. And there were some real fine musicians in there, Sam Bird, Ridge Stewart, Aida Whitley. I can't remember the trumpet players, but they had done that. Anyway, I just had all these offers. Everything was done by telegram. The guys, they'd wire you and say, have a nice job, $60 a week or $50 a week or whatever. Must have done that. So I decided to take several of those jobs, and I did. And I just stayed for maybe six weeks, two months, and I'd go. Always end up back in the street with the Buddies from the other, but they'd always continued to me. Now, I'll get into some things I think would be more interesting to. The Louisiana Rounders were organized by Pat and Bob DeQueer, who were from New Iberia. And they originally called themselves the original Jazzland Six. And in the twenties, they played all over Southern Louisiana. They were the earliest white musicians I ever heard who really played black. I mean, in the exact style of Southern Louisiana black musicians. They were tremendous. But we didn't realize how good they worked until late years. And so, they actually came to El Dorado, Arkansas, and played in the oil fields for just a short time. And then they came over to Shreveport and organized the Louisiana Rambles. Well, this was under a piano player named Bob Canfield, but it was a kind of a band that all the people shared in, and they were all that's familiar. And they developed into, in my idea, the best big band that we ever had in that part of the country. They had Bert Sigerson from New Orleans, a name you may not be at all familiar with, a great tenor saxophone player, still living as far as I know, and lived in New Orleans. And, Pat and Bob, Pat played trumpet, Bob played trumpet, Bob. They had a wonderful drummer named Norm Landry. Norm is now still living and playing in Houston, Texas. And Pat and Bob were both there. Bob Canfield was there. But anyway, they had always wanted me to join them. I preferred to play one-nighters on the roads in small towns and another half-clun. But they finally taught me into joining the band, because I did after the Hotel Washington in Shreveport. And that was some of the best chords I ever did, if I think it was good, worth the round of the chords. But we had over a hundred arrangements committed to memory. We could just knock them off, you know. Nobody had any music. And, but we had hard arrangements and played them well. So, I went on from the Ramblers after they broke up. I went out to California and played, but that's when I first played with Jack. I had met him in Shreveport and we became fast friends. But he was with Doc Ross' band out in Los Angeles. So, he wired for me to come. I drove 2,000 miles out to play with Jack. Two Doc Ross' jazz bandits. But, I had married in the meantime. And, I had to stay in California for a short time. Claiborne Bryson was organizing a band to open at the Jure Hotel that spring. And, he had most of the old ramblers with him. And, so, he called me and cried and he wanted to come back to me for his kid. And, this takes us up to about 1926. And, well, there was a music store opening in the street for Okahop Music Fund. It was referring very much like Werleim's. They had a cool store chain. They were very good people. And, I had decided then that I couldn't be very happy to marry me on the road. And, music business is best is always a hard way to make a living. So, I decided I wanted to go in the music store. I'd been hanging around the music stores from the time I was 13, 14 years old. In the hometown. They would let me talk and do a little bit chores. And, the drummer with the little bands that were playing locally was the chief salesman for this company. So, I just went into the music stores. And, I guess that was when I was like, and I went back to playing a number of different times. And, I played weekends for 20 years with various combinations. Always generally in the open city and which store, wherever. We were always the best union bands. Strictly union. And, of course, had the pleasure of jamming with incoming musicians. And, Dick, I'm kind of, actually kind of a historian of jazz myself. It's a hobby with me. And, I just always kept up with it, like some guys do baseball and other things these times. And, I might not have been able to tell you who was president that year, but I could tell you who played Cristalpa as Duke Ellington. That type of thing. So, it's just always been a wonderful, fascinating thing for me. And, I've continued it. I had a good pleasure to play with people like, started with people like Jack and Winnie. Dan Flossman was one of my real first friends. And, we played together in the school court in 1943. And, it's a long, I could burn for hours. But, I just, it's just been always fun for me. And, I've kept it up a little bit. Maybe I sneak five minutes in the office or at home. I don't get to practice any length of time, because there's always something else to do, you know, like these guitars or whatever. But, I always managed to keep it up enough where I could play the Tin Roof Blues pretty good with Howard. Is that right, Hal?
